title: Java Memory Model
scopeHtml: Happens-before, visibility vs atomicity vs ordering, volatile, final and safe publication, double-checked locking, false sharing, VarHandle modes and immutability, for senior JVM backend interviews.

questions.promptHtml: Concurrency bugs are usually described as visibility, atomicity or ordering problems. Explain each, and say which Java tools fix which.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who say "thread safety" without separating these three cannot choose between volatile, synchronized and atomics. This is the vocabulary test.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Visibility is whether one thread's write can be seen by another thread at all. Atomicity is whether a multi-step operation can be observed half-done or interleaved. Ordering is whether the sequence of writes that another thread sees matches program order. volatile fixes visibility and ordering but not atomicity of compound actions. synchronized and locks fix all three. Atomics (AtomicInteger) give atomic single-variable read-modify-write plus volatile-style visibility.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each core has registers, store buffers and caches, and the JIT compiler keeps values in registers. A plain write by thread A may sit in A's store buffer or be eliminated by the compiler, so thread B never sees it. That is visibility. Separately, count++ compiles to read, add, write. Two threads can both read 5 and both write 6. That is atomicity. Finally, the compiler and the CPU may reorder independent stores, so B may see ready = true before data = 42. That is ordering.

Problem Example Fix
Visibility while(!stop){} never ends volatile, lock, atomic
Atomicity count++, check-then-act synchronized, Lock, AtomicInteger, CAS
Ordering flag seen before data volatile flag, lock, final

The Java Memory Model (JMM, JLS chapter 17) answers all three with one abstraction: the happens-before relation. If action A happens-before action B, then A's effects are visible to B and ordered before it. Without a happens-before edge between a write and a read, the read may see the write, an older value, or (for racy code) surprising ones.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Flags {
    boolean stop;          // visibility bug: reader may spin forever
    volatile boolean ok;   // visibility + ordering, fine for a flag
    int count;             // count++ not atomic even if volatile

    final AtomicInteger safeCount = new AtomicInteger(); // atomic RMW
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "volatile makes it thread-safe". It makes single reads and writes visible and ordered, nothing compound.
  • Thinking visibility problems need multiple CPUs. The JIT can hoist a read out of a loop on a single core.
  • Treating the three as independent. Locks give all three because unlock/lock forms one happens-before edge.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does volatile int make i++ safe? → No. It is read, increment, write; use AtomicInteger or a lock.
  2. Can a program have no atomicity problem and still be wrong? → Yes, visibility alone: a single plain write that another thread never sees.
  3. Why does the JMM talk about happens-before instead of "flush to main memory"? → Hardware has no single "main memory flush" step and compilers also reorder; happens-before is a hardware-independent contract (JLS 17.4.5).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "volatile for visibility, synchronized for atomicity". The senior answer adds that synchronized also gives visibility and ordering, names compiler and CPU as separate causes, and frames everything as happens-before.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A background refresher thread updating a plain Map field that request threads read can leave stale config for hours on some JIT-compiled paths, and is easily mistaken for a cache TTL bug.

questions.promptHtml: What exactly does volatile guarantee in Java, and what does it not guarantee?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: volatile is the most misused keyword. The signal is whether you know it is a happens-before edge, not a lock.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that field. So the reader sees that write and everything the writer did before it. All volatile accesses are also in a single total order, and volatile long/double accesses are atomic. It does not make compound actions like i++ or check-then-act atomic, and it gives no mutual exclusion.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rules from JLS 17.4.4/17.7: a write to volatile v synchronizes-with every later read of v; volatile reads and writes of 64-bit values are atomic; the JIT may not cache a volatile in a register across reads.

The "piggybacking" effect is the useful part: writes before the volatile write become visible to a thread after it reads the volatile.

Thread A                  Thread B
data = 42;      (plain)
ready = true;   (volatile write) ----hb----> if (ready)   (volatile read)
                                               print(data)  // sees 42

Volatile is one-directional publication of a state. It is right for: stop flags, publishing an immutable object reference, a status that has a single writer. It is wrong for counters with several writers and for invariants spanning two variables.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Worker implements Runnable {
    private volatile boolean running = true;
    public void stop() { running = false; }
    public void run() { while (running) { doWork(); } }
}

// Broken: two volatile fields do not make an atomic pair
volatile int lo, hi;                 // invariant lo <= hi can be violated
void setRange(int l, int h){ lo = l; hi = h; } // reader may see new lo, old hi

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• volatile on a reference does not make the pointed object's fields volatile; mutating it is still unsynchronized.
  • volatile arrays: only the reference is volatile, not elements (see the volatile array scenario later in this chunk).
  • Using volatile as a cheap lock for "check then init".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Volatile vs AtomicInteger? → Atomic adds CAS-based read-modify-write; volatile has only read and write.
  2. Is a volatile write cheap? → Cheaper than a lock but not free; see the cost question in this chunk.
  3. Does volatile give mutual exclusion? → No; two threads can both pass a volatile check and both act.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "reads go to main memory". Senior: happens-before edge, piggybacking of prior writes, total order among volatiles, 64-bit atomicity, and the single-writer pattern as the safe use.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "volatile int inFlight; inFlight++" in a rate limiter drifted by thousands under load and let through far more traffic than configured.

questions.promptHtml: Besides mutual exclusion, what does synchronized do for memory visibility? Why does reading a variable inside synchronized matter even if you only read?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many people think synchronized is only about locking. Knowing it is a release/acquire pair explains why unsynchronized readers of a locked writer are buggy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Unlocking a monitor happens-before every later lock of the same monitor. So everything thread A wrote before releasing the lock is visible to thread B after acquiring the same lock. It only works if both sides use the same lock object. A reader that skips the lock gets no guarantee.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The monitor unlock is a release and the lock is an acquire. JIT and CPU may not move accesses out of the critical section in the dangerous direction, but they may move accesses into it (the "roach motel" rule, so code before the lock may sink in and code after the unlock may move in). Lock coarsening relies on that.

A: lock(m); x=1; y=2; unlock(m)  --hb-->  B: lock(m); read x,y; unlock(m)
A: lock(m); x=1; unlock(m)           B: read x  (no lock) -> NO guarantee

Consequence: getters of a class whose setters are synchronized must also be synchronized (or the field volatile). Java 8 vs later: biased locking was disabled by default in JDK 15 and removed in later releases (JEP 374, verify exact removal release); it does not change JMM semantics.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Counter {
    private int n;
    synchronized void inc() { n++; }
    synchronized int get() { return n; }   // needed for visibility, not just atomicity
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Synchronized setter plus unsynchronized getter.
  • Locking on different objects (this in one method, a private lock in another) and assuming an edge exists.
  • Locking on a value that changes (synchronized(count) on a boxed Integer reassigned each time).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does synchronized guarantee ordering inside the block? → Not ordering from the viewpoint of unsynchronized threads, only for threads that lock the same monitor.
  2. Can code move into a critical section? → Yes, the compiler may; code may not move out across the boundary in the dangerous direction.
  3. Does wait() give visibility? → It releases and re-acquires the monitor, so yes, with the same edges.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "only one thread at a time". Senior: release/acquire edge per monitor, same-lock requirement, and roach-motel reordering.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A read path skipped the lock "because it is only a read" and returned partially updated state after a refactor, visible only on a 64-core host.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a data race and a race condition? Can you have one without the other?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The terms are used interchangeably in standups but the JMM defines only data races. The distinction shows you can reason formally.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A data race is a memory-model term: two threads access the same variable, at least one writes, and no happens-before edge orders them. A race condition is a logic bug where correctness depends on timing, for example check-then-act. You can have either without the other: a race on a volatile counter is not a data race but is a race condition; a benign racy read can be a data race with no logic bug.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
JLS 17.4.5 defines a data race as conflicting accesses not ordered by happens-before. If a program has no data races in any sequentially consistent execution, it is "correctly synchronized" and all executions look sequentially consistent (SC-DRF). So eliminating data races gives you simple reasoning; it does not eliminate race conditions.

Data race Race condition
Defined by JMM / hardware visibility Application invariant
Example plain int written and read by two threads if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) on a ConcurrentHashMap
Fix add hb edge make the compound action atomic

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// No data race (all access volatile), still a race condition:
volatile int balance = 100;
void withdraw(int a){ if (balance >= a) balance -= a; } // two threads overdraw

// Fix: atomic compound action
AtomicInteger bal = new AtomicInteger(100);
boolean withdraw2(int a){
    int cur;
    do { cur = bal.get(); if (cur < a) return false; }
    while (!bal.compareAndSet(cur, cur - a));
    return true;
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring everything volatile and calling the class thread-safe.
  • Calling a data race "benign" without understanding word tearing and JIT hoisting.
  • Believing a concurrent collection removes race conditions across two calls.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is ConcurrentHashMap.get then put safe? → Individual calls are, the pair is a race condition; use putIfAbsent/computeIfAbsent.
  2. Can a data race corrupt the JVM? → No; Java guarantees type safety and no out-of-thin-air values, effects are limited to which values reads observe (JLS 17.4.5).
  3. How do you find data races in tests? → Tools such as jcstress for targeted models; ThreadSanitizer does not target the JVM.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: both mean "threads step on each other". Senior: formal split, SC-DRF, and knows volatile removes data races but not logic races.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Duplicate payment attempts came from a check-then-act on a thread-safe map; no JMM tool would have flagged it.

questions.contextHtml:
A batch job runs a worker thread and a main thread. In staging with -Xint it terminates. In production on JDK 17 (C2 compiled) the process hangs forever after "stopping worker" is logged. Thread dump shows the worker RUNNABLE at Worker.run using 100% of one core.

class Worker implements Runnable {
    private boolean stopped = false;
    long processed;
    public void run() {
        while (!stopped) { processed++; }
    }
    void stop() { stopped = true; }
}
// main: t.start(); Thread.sleep(5000); w.stop(); log("stopping worker"); t.join();
questions.promptHtml: Why does it hang and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add Thread.sleep in the loop" or "make it synchronized everywhere" without explaining. Or blaming the OS scheduler.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it reproduce only after warm-up (JIT)? Does -Xint or a debug breakpoint hide it? Is there any other write to stopped? Those separate visibility from logic.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart with the job killed; as an emergency patch declare stopped volatile.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) JIT hoisted the read of stopped out of the loop, (b) worker thread starved (unlikely, 100% CPU shows it runs), (c) deadlock (no: RUNNABLE, no locks).
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack shows RUNNABLE in the loop; run with -XX:+PrintCompilation to see Worker::run compiled by C2 (OSR); rerun with -Xint to see it stop; or JFR to confirm the thread is hot at the loop.
  5. Root cause: The write in stop() and the read in run() have no happens-before edge, so this is a data race. The JMM allows the compiler to read stopped once and treat the loop as while(true). A loop body with no synchronization gives C2 licence to hoist it.
  6. Fix: short-term private volatile boolean stopped. Better, use interruption: while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) and call t.interrupt().
  7. Prevention: code-review rule: any field read by a loop and written by another thread must be volatile or guarded; use jcstress or review checklists; SpotBugs flags some of these (IS2_INCONSISTENT_SYNC).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add Thread.sleep(1) as a fix; it can hide the bug and is not guaranteed to create an edge (the JLS says sleep has no synchronization semantics).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did it work in debug mode? → The interpreter re-reads memory each iteration; the bug appears only after JIT compilation.
  • What if processed is also read from main after join? → join creates a happens-before edge from the thread's last action, so that read is safe.
  • What if I call System.out.println inside the loop? → It synchronizes internally, which may accidentally create edges and mask the bug; do not rely on it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shutdown hook flipped a plain boolean to drain a consumer loop. It worked in every test for two years; after a JDK upgrade changed inlining, pods hung on termination until the orchestrator killed them at the 30 s grace period.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests sleeps or "restart it"; cannot explain why debug mode behaves differently.
  • Hire: identifies missing visibility, adds volatile, mentions JIT hoisting.
  • Strong hire: also names the data race formally, prefers interruption, explains why sleep is not a fix, and proposes a detection practice.

questions.promptHtml: List the happens-before rules in the Java Memory Model and explain what "happens-before" does and does not mean.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the core of the JMM. Seniors should enumerate the edges and know it is about visibility, not wall-clock time.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Happens-before is a partial order: if A happens-before B, A's effects are visible to B and ordered before it. Edges: program order within a thread; monitor unlock to later lock of the same monitor; volatile write to later read of that variable; Thread.start() to the first action of the started thread; the last action of a thread to a successful join() or isAlive()==false in another; an interrupt call to detection of the interrupt; and transitivity. It does not mean A executes earlier in time, only that if B reads, it must see A's effects.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
JLS 17.4.4 defines synchronizes-with edges, 17.4.5 builds happens-before from program order plus those edges plus transitivity. The JLS also lists the end of a constructor happening-before the start of the finalizer. The java.util.concurrent package documentation adds library edges (verify in the java.util.concurrent package summary "Memory Consistency Properties"):

  • Actions before submitting a task to an Executor happen-before the task's execution.
  • Actions in a task happen-before Future.get() returns.
  • Actions before putting an item into a BlockingQueue/ConcurrentMap happen-before the actions after taking/getting it.
  • CountDownLatch.countDown() happens-before a return from await().
Thread A: x = 1; ---- start()/volatile/unlock ----> Thread B: reads x (sees 1)
Without an edge: B may see 0 or 1; no guarantee.

Happens-before does not forbid reordering that is invisible. The JLS says the implementation may reorder as long as the result matches a legal execution.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
int a;
Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(a)); // sees 5
a = 5;
t.start();   // start edge: write before start is visible in t

ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
a = 6;
Future<Integer> f = ex.submit(() -> a + 1); // submit edge

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading it as "A ran before B in real time". Even with A earlier on the clock, no edge means no guarantee.
  • Forgetting that the edge is per variable/monitor: locking different monitors creates nothing.
  • Assuming Thread.sleep or System.currentTimeMillis ordering creates an edge.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does ConcurrentHashMap.put happen-before a later get of the same key? → Yes, per the package documentation.
  2. Is there an edge between a Thread.sleep end and another thread? → No.
  3. Can happens-before be violated by the JIT? → Only in ways no legal observer can detect; the contract is on observable behavior.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average names volatile and synchronized. Senior lists thread start/join, executor, queue and latch edges, uses transitivity to prove a design, and stresses "visible, not earlier".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team passed a mutable config object to a pool task and mutated it after submit; the edge covers writes before submit only, so workers saw random mixes.

questions.promptHtml: Who reorders instructions in a Java program, and what rules limit it? Why does it not break single-threaded code?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It explains why "it works on my machine" concurrency bugs exist. Seniors can name the three layers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Three layers reorder: the javac/JIT compiler, the CPU (out-of-order execution and store buffers), and the cache system. Single-threaded code is protected by as-if-serial semantics: any reordering must give the same result as program order for that thread. Other threads get no such promise unless a happens-before edge exists. Volatile, locks and final-field freeze insert compiler and hardware barriers to restrict reordering.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: data = 42; ready = true; touch independent variables, so as-if-serial lets them swap. A second thread that sees ready == true may then read old data.

Hardware differences matter. x86 (TSO) only lets a later load pass an earlier store to a different address (StoreLoad); ARM and POWER allow most reorderings. Shipilev's experiments on JDK 8 showed unsafe publication failing on ARM Cortex-A9 and only rarely on x86 under stress flags. So code can pass years on x86 and break on ARM instances.

Barrier types: LoadLoad, LoadStore, StoreStore, StoreLoad. The JIT emits what the target needs. A volatile write generally needs the expensive StoreLoad after it on x86.

The JMM defines legal reorderings through happens-before and "roach motel" for locks, not through barriers; barriers are an implementation detail.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Publisher {
    int data; boolean ready;            // broken: plain fields
    void write() { data = 42; ready = true; }
    void read()  { if (ready) use(data); } // may see data == 0
}
// Fix: volatile boolean ready;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing reordering is only a CPU issue; the JIT is the more common cause.
  • Testing on x86 laptops only, then deploying to Graviton/ARM.
  • Explaining it with "main memory flush" rather than edges.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is as-if-serial? → Within one thread, results must look like program order.
  2. What reordering does x86 allow? → StoreLoad only (store buffer), per Intel's memory model; verify against Intel SDM if asked.
  3. Why does volatile fix the example? → The volatile write is a release, the read an acquire; data = 42 cannot move after the write and the read cannot move before.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "CPU may reorder". Senior: compiler vs CPU, as-if-serial, x86 vs ARM differences, and why testing on one architecture proves nothing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service moved from x86 to ARM instances for cost and began failing a few times per million requests because of unsafe publication that had never failed before.

questions.promptHtml: Explain double-checked locking for lazy singletons. Why was it broken before Java 5, and what makes it correct now?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic. It tests understanding of partial construction and volatile semantics together.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: DCL checks a field without a lock, then locks and checks again before creating. Without volatile, instance = new Foo() can be reordered so the reference is stored before the constructor's writes are visible, so another thread sees a non-null, half-built object. Since Java 5 (JSR-133), declaring the field volatile makes it correct. The better choices are the initialization-on-demand holder or an enum.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
instance = new Foo() is three steps: allocate, run constructor, assign reference. The compiler or CPU may assign the reference before the constructor writes are visible to others. The fast path reads instance with no lock, so there is no edge and the thread sees a non-null reference to an object whose fields may still be default.

With volatile, the write of the reference is a release: constructor writes cannot be reordered after it, and the unlocked read is an acquire. Shipilev measured the unsafe variant failing on x86 at a very low rate and on ARM far more often (43.8K failures in 3.7G tries on x86 with stress flags; hundreds per 100M on ARMv7).

Alternatives:

  • Holder idiom: class initialization is guarded by a JVM lock and gives an edge, lazy and lock-free after init.
  • enum singleton.
  • Local variable DCL: copy volatile to a local to read it once on the fast path.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Config {
    private static volatile Config instance;
    static Config get() {
        Config c = instance;           // one volatile read
        if (c == null) {
            synchronized (Config.class) {
                c = instance;
                if (c == null) instance = c = new Config();
            }
        }
        return c;
    }
}
// Holder idiom: no volatile, no lock
class Config2 {
    private static class H { static final Config2 I = new Config2(); }
    static Config2 get() { return H.I; }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Omitting volatile ("it works in tests").
  • Believing synchronized on the inner block alone fixes the outer unsynchronized read.
  • Using DCL on a field of a mutable object where later fields are set after publishing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does DCL work if all fields of Config are final? → Yes, final-field semantics make it safe even without volatile for the object's contents, but the reference race remains for readers seeing null, which only makes them take the lock path (verify with your exact class design).
  2. Why prefer the holder? → Simpler, no volatile read cost, JVM-guaranteed.
  3. Why use a local variable? → One volatile read on the fast path instead of two.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "add volatile". Senior: explains the three-step construction, the edge on the read side, ARM vs x86 failure rates, and picks holder or enum.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hand-rolled lazy pool factory without volatile gave a null ObjectMapper field in rare requests after warmup on a new CPU architecture.

questions.promptHtml: What special guarantee do final fields have in the JMM? What are the conditions, and when does it fail?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the foundation of safe immutable objects and a subtle area where this escape breaks everything.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: When a constructor finishes, the JVM performs a freeze on its final fields. Any thread that gets a reference to the object, even through a data race, sees the correctly initialized final fields and the objects reachable through them as of the freeze. It fails if this escapes during construction, if the fields are not final, or if someone modifies them with reflection.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
JLS 17.5: the guarantee applies to threads that see the reference only after the constructor completes. Reads of final fields and of what they point to (for example the contents of a final int[] filled in the constructor) are covered. Non-final fields in the same object are not covered unless some other edge exists. Per Shipilev's notes, HotSpot implements this with a barrier at the end of constructors that write final fields, which in practice also covers the other fields written there (an implementation detail, do not rely on it).

Failures:

  • this escape: registering a listener or starting a thread in the constructor lets another thread see a not-yet-frozen object.
  • Mutable state inside: final reference to a HashMap that is mutated after construction is not protected.
  • Reflection or Unsafe writes to final fields.
  • Final does not guarantee the reader sees the reference at all; it may still read null from the racy field.
Thread A: new Obj(){ final x=3; int y=4 }; shared = obj  (racy)
Thread B: o = shared; if (o != null) { o.x == 3 (guaranteed), o.y may be 0 }

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
final class Point {
    private final int x, y;
    private final List<String> tags;
    Point(int x, int y, List<String> t) {
        this.x = x; this.y = y;
        this.tags = List.copyOf(t);   // immutable snapshot
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking final means "visible immediately for any type of field in the class".
  • Escaping this through a lambda or inner class in the constructor.
  • Making a field final but holding a mutable collection.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a record's component get final semantics? → Yes, record fields are final.
  2. Is a static final field safe? → Yes via class initialization edges.
  3. Can I set a final field with reflection? → Technically possible for instance fields via setAccessible; records and hidden classes forbid it, and JIT may have constant-folded already.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "final means immutable". Senior: freeze action, applies only after constructor end, covers reachable state, fails on this escape, and does not fix publication of the reference itself.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A metrics registry object subscribed itself to an event bus in its constructor and a worker saw a null final name, producing NPEs only under load.

questions.promptHtml: What is safe publication, and what are the idioms to achieve it in Java?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Safe publication is how most real code passes objects between threads. Interviewers want to see you can name idioms and spot violations.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Safe publication means the reference and the object's state both become visible to another thread in a correct order. The idioms: initialize in a static initializer, store the reference in a volatile field or AtomicReference, store it in a field guarded by a lock, store it in a final field of a properly constructed object, or hand it through a thread-safe collection or queue or executor. If the object is effectively immutable, publication must still be safe; if it is mutable, it also needs ongoing synchronization.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each idiom produces a happens-before edge between the writer of the reference and the reader (JLS 17.4.4; java.util.concurrent documentation for collections).

Idiom Edge source
static initializer / holder class init lock
volatile / AtomicReference volatile write-read
lock-guarded field unlock-lock
final field wrapper freeze
ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue, Executor.submit library documented edges

Unsafe publication example: this.cache = new Cache(data) into a plain field read by another thread. The reader may see null, or a non-null Cache with default-valued non-final fields. For an effectively immutable object (fields never changed after construction, but not declared final), safe publication is the only protection.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Holder {
    private volatile ImmutableConfig cfg = ImmutableConfig.load(); // safe: volatile
    void reload() { cfg = ImmutableConfig.load(); }                // atomic swap
    ImmutableConfig get() { return cfg; }
}
// Unsafe: plain field
class Bad { ImmutableConfig cfg; void reload(){ cfg = ImmutableConfig.load(); } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a plain static field written from main thread and read by workers after "later" thread start (start edge covers only writes before start).
  • Assuming effectively immutable beans are safe without an edge.
  • Publishing this in the constructor (not safe, state not yet complete).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a HashMap field written once at startup and read afterward safe? → Only if reads happen after an edge such as start/join/volatile/final publish.
  2. Does a ThreadLocal need publication? → No, it is confined to a thread.
  3. Is publication through a static non-final field safe? → No, only initialization in the static initializer itself is.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists "use volatile". Senior lists all idioms with their edge, distinguishes safe publication from thread-safety, and ties it to effective immutability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hot-reload thread assigned a new routing table to a plain field. Most requests were fine; a few saw partially built tables after JIT optimized reads.

questions.contextHtml:
A rate limiter in an API gateway (8 pods, 4 vCPU each, 20k RPS peak) enforces 100 requests/second per tenant. After a load test, tenant quotas are exceeded by ~15% and the dashboard counter value does not match access logs.

class TenantLimiter {
    private volatile int used;
    private volatile long windowStart = System.currentTimeMillis();
    boolean tryAcquire() {
        long now = System.currentTimeMillis();
        if (now - windowStart >= 1000) { used = 0; windowStart = now; }
        if (used < 100) { used++; return true; }
        return false;
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it without adding a global lock?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "volatile is already there, so it must be the clock" or "wrap it in synchronized" without discussing contention or window reset races.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Per tenant instance or shared? Accuracy requirement (hard or approximate limit)? Is it per pod or cluster wide?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Lower limit by the observed error margin, or put the limiter behind synchronized on a per-tenant object, which at 100 ops/s is cheap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) used++ is a read-modify-write on a volatile, not atomic; (b) check used < 100 then increment is check-then-act; (c) window reset races, two threads both zero and set start; (d) clock jumps (red herring unless NTP step).
  4. How I'd verify each: Write a jcstress or a stress test with 16 threads on a tenant; compare allowed count to 100; inspect with a JFR lock profile that there is none; review atomic bytecode (getfield, iadd, putfield).
  5. Root cause: Volatile gives visibility, not atomicity. Two threads read used == 99, both pass the check, both write 100 and 100, a lost update and an over-admit.
  6. Fix: Short-term, synchronized per tenant limiter. Long-term, make the state one immutable object swapped by CAS, or use an AtomicLong that packs window and count, or a LongAdder-style approximation if a few percent error is acceptable. Use System.nanoTime() for elapsed time.
  7. Prevention: A lint rule against volatile with ++/+= (SpotBugs VO_VOLATILE_INCREMENT); concurrency tests in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use one global lock (contention across tenants); I would not rely on volatile long to protect a two-field invariant.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if pods are 8 and limit is global? → Local limiters multiply the limit; need a shared store such as Redis token bucket, owned by other chunks.
  • Could AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet alone fix it? → It fixes the counter but not check-then-act or the window reset; still needs CAS loop or lock.
  • Does LongAdder help? → Cheaper increments under contention but cannot enforce a hard cap precisely.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A quota service "fixed" overuse by making the counter volatile. Overuse dropped only because the extra memory fence slowed threads; the root issue remained until the check-then-act became one CAS.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says volatile should be enough; adds sleeps.
  • Hire: identifies non-atomic increment and check-then-act, fixes with atomic or lock.
  • Strong hire: also finds the window reset race, uses nanoTime, discusses contention per tenant vs global, and proposes a test.

questions.promptHtml: Is reading and writing a long atomic in Java? What is word tearing and does Java allow it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know the JLS has a specific exception for 64-bit values and what the guarantees are for neighbouring fields.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For non-volatile long and double, the JLS permits a write to be split into two 32-bit writes, so a racing reader can see half of one value and half of another. Volatile long/double accesses are always atomic, and references are always atomic. Word tearing, where a write to one field or array element clobbers a neighbouring one, is forbidden by Java: each field and array element is independent.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
JLS 17.7: non-volatile 64-bit writes may be treated as two writes; implementations are encouraged to avoid this and programmers to use volatile or synchronize. In practice, 64-bit HotSpot on mainstream hardware does the access atomically, but that is not a language guarantee (Shipilev notes the exception could be dropped, and it is hardware dependent for aligned vs misaligned access).

JLS 17.6 forbids word tearing: a JVM on hardware without byte stores may not implement byteArr[i] = x as read-modify-write of a word. So two threads writing different byte[] elements need no synchronization to avoid clobbering. They still need an edge to see each other's writes.

Type Atomic read/write?
int, float, boolean, reference yes
long, double non-volatile not guaranteed
long, double volatile yes
i++, x += y never atomic

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Stats {
    long total;            // may tear on a racy read (spec), fine in practice on x64
    volatile long safe;    // atomic read/write guaranteed
    final byte[] flags = new byte[8];
    // Two threads writing flags[0] and flags[1] do not interfere (no word tearing)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using volatile "to be safe" and then doing total += x, which is still not atomic.
  • Assuming 64-bit JVM means atomic by language guarantee.
  • Confusing word tearing (neighbouring data) with long tearing (same variable).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not make every long volatile? → Ordering cost and no gain for single-thread data.
  2. Is AtomicLong.get atomic? → Yes, it wraps a volatile long.
  3. Do LongAdder reads give an atomic snapshot? → No, sum() is not an atomic snapshot of concurrent updates.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "long writes might be non-atomic". Senior adds volatile fix, word-tearing prohibition, the practical 64-bit behaviour, and that spec guarantees still matter for portable code.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A unix-millis timestamp stored in a plain long and updated by a refresher produced rare absurd values on a 32-bit embedded JVM, a case the team had never tested.

questions.contextHtml:
An internal library publishes pricing events. After upgrading to a 16-core node, about 1 in 200,000 events processed by the listener throws NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "this.region" is null. Stack points to PriceFeed.onTick, called by the dispatcher thread, never from the constructing thread.

public class PriceFeed implements TickListener {
    private final String region;
    private final Map<String, Double> prices = new HashMap<>();

    public PriceFeed(String region, Bus bus) {
        bus.register(this);        // dispatcher thread starts delivering ticks
        this.region = region;
        // ... more setup
    }
    public void onTick(Tick t) { prices.put(t.sym(), t.px()); log(region.length()); }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug and explain why final does not save you.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make region volatile" or "add a null check", without noticing the register(this) before assignment.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the bus deliver on its own thread? Does registration start delivery immediately? Is it one-in-N frequent only at startup?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a start-up gate so the bus ignores ticks until the feed is registered after construction; or catch and drop early ticks.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) this escapes in the constructor; (b) bus delivers messages that were buffered; (c) classloading race (unlikely); (d) wrong region config (red herring because it is intermittent).
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the constructor order; reproduce with a delay after register in a test; confirm with a stack trace that the failing thread is the dispatcher; jcstress test of the construct-and-publish pattern.
  5. Root cause: this was published to another thread before the constructor finished. The final-field freeze (JLS 17.5) happens at constructor end, so the guarantee does not apply, and even logically region is not yet assigned. Reading it gives null.
  6. Fix: Use a static factory: construct fully, then register.
public static PriceFeed create(String region, Bus bus) {
    PriceFeed f = new PriceFeed(region);
    bus.register(f);                 // after construction; bus registration should publish safely
    return f;
}

Also replace the HashMap with a ConcurrentHashMap, because onTick runs on another thread. 7. Prevention: Static analysis for this passed from constructors (IntelliJ and Error Prone have checks, verify names), a team rule: no registration or thread start in constructors. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not mark the field volatile; the problem is publication ordering, not the field type. I would not add a null check and ship it, since prices is also visibly broken.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if I register in init() called by Spring after construction? → Fine if the container publishes safely; the bean is fully constructed before the call.
  • Is an inner-class or lambda in the constructor the same bug? → Yes, they capture this.
  • Would the bug show if the listener ran on the same thread? → No; same-thread program order lets it observe the assignments that precede it, not those after.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A subscription class started a polling thread in its constructor. The bug lived for a year because most subclasses finished construction before the first poll; only a slow subclass constructor exposed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds null check or volatile.
  • Hire: identifies this-escape and the factory fix.
  • Strong hire: ties it to the final-field freeze rule, spots the unsafe HashMap, and proposes a lint/review rule.

questions.promptHtml: How expensive is a volatile read or write? Does it differ between x86 and ARM?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors must reason about performance of synchronization without folklore ("volatile is slow" or "volatile is free").

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A volatile read on x86 is an ordinary load with compiler restrictions, so it is nearly free except it blocks some optimizations such as keeping the value in a register. A volatile write needs a StoreLoad barrier after it on x86, typically a locked instruction, costing tens of cycles. On ARM, HotSpot uses load-acquire and store-release style instructions (verify the exact instruction for your JDK), so both sides have some cost. The bigger costs are contended cache lines and lost optimizations, not the barrier alone.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
x86's TSO model already provides LoadLoad, LoadStore and StoreStore ordering. Only StoreLoad (store buffer drain) is missing, and HotSpot emits it after volatile stores (a lock addl or similar). So hot loops that write a volatile each iteration pay for draining the store buffer; reads in loops cannot be hoisted.

On weaker models (ARM, POWER), the compiler must emit explicit ordering for both volatile loads and stores. JDK 8+ AArch64 uses ldar/stlr (verify per JDK version).

Practical sense of cost (order of magnitude, verify with JMH on your hardware):

  • uncontended volatile read: about a normal load
  • volatile write: about 10 to 40 cycles plus drained store buffer
  • contended write across cores: cache-line transfer, hundreds of cycles

Rules of thumb: a single-writer volatile read-mostly field is cheap; a shared volatile counter written by all cores is a bottleneck due to coherence traffic, not the fence itself. For single-writer cases, setRelease via VarHandle or AtomicX.lazySet avoids the full barrier (see the VarHandle question).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Read-mostly: cheap
volatile Config cfg;          // one writer, many readers

// Write-heavy contention: use LongAdder, not volatile++
LongAdder hits = new LongAdder();
hits.increment();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Removing volatile "for speed" without measuring, creating a visibility bug.
  • Microbenchmarking volatile without JMH (JIT removes the code).
  • Ignoring false sharing around hot volatile fields.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a volatile read inhibit optimization? → Compiler cannot keep it in a register across loop iterations nor reorder surrounding accesses past it.
  2. Is synchronized slower than volatile? → Uncontended, a lock is more expensive but usually fine; contention dominates.
  3. How would you measure it? → JMH with -prof perfasm on Linux to see the emitted instructions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "volatile is slower than normal fields". Senior: separates barrier cost from contention, x86 vs ARM, and picks single-writer/release patterns.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A tracing library put a volatile write on every span start; on a 64-core box this created a coherence hot spot visible as CPU in Tracer.start in async-profiler.

questions.promptHtml: Why is immutability the simplest concurrency strategy on the JVM, and what traps remain when you say "this class is immutable"?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Immutability appears in every senior design review. The signal is whether you know the real requirements, not "make fields final".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An immutable object cannot change after construction, so it needs no locks, can be shared freely, and is safe to cache. For real immutability: all fields final, no this escape, the class cannot be subclassed (or is final), mutable inputs and outputs are defensively copied, and the fields themselves reference immutable types. Records give final fields but are shallow: a record holding a List is not deeply immutable. You still need safe publication of the reference unless all fields are final.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two reasons it works: no write after freeze means no race on the contents; final-field semantics (JLS 17.5) give safe visibility even through racy publication.

Checklist:

  1. final class or private constructors.
  2. private final fields.
  3. No setters; "withers" return new instances.
  4. Copy mutable constructor args (List.copyOf, Date clone, array clone).
  5. Don't return internal mutable state.
  6. Don't leak this.

Trade-offs: allocation churn on frequent updates (young GC absorbs most of it), copying cost for big structures (use persistent data structures such as Vavr or Kotlin persistent collections, or copy-on-write with a volatile swap), and awkward mutation APIs.

Kotlin: val is only read-only reference; List<T> is a read-only view that may be backed by a mutable list; data class copy is shallow.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
public record Order(String id, List<String> items) {
    public Order { items = List.copyOf(items); }   // defensive, immutable copy
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Final fields holding a mutable ArrayList/Date/array.
  • Collections.unmodifiableList(list) is a view; the underlying list can still change.
  • Subclass overrides getters and breaks immutability.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. List.of vs Collections.unmodifiableList? → List.of is a real immutable copy (null-hostile); unmodifiable is a view.
  2. How do you update an immutable shared config? → Build a new instance and swap one volatile or AtomicReference.
  3. Is an immutable class always cheaper to use? → No; large objects updated per request create allocation and copying overhead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "make fields final". Senior: lists all conditions, defensive copies, shallow records, publication rules, and the swap-the-snapshot pattern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "immutable" settings record wrapped a mutable Map from a YAML library; a reload thread mutated it and request threads threw ConcurrentModificationException.

questions.contextHtml: A pricing service has a RateTable of ~50,000 entries, read on every request (6,000 RPS, 8 cores, each request does 5 lookups) and rebuilt from a database every 30 seconds by a scheduler thread. Today the code uses a synchronized method for both read and refresh; p99 is 90 ms and profiling shows RateTable.get blocked threads (JFR lock profile: 35% of samples waiting on one monitor, refresh holds the lock for ~300 ms while rebuilding).
questions.promptHtml: How would you restructure it, and what are the memory-model implications of each option?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use ReadWriteLock" without noting that refresh still blocks readers for 300 ms, or "make it volatile" without separating building from publishing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must all lookups in one request see the same version? Tolerable staleness (30 s vs 1 s)? Table size growth? Does refresh sometimes fail?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Build the new map outside the lock and only swap the reference inside it; that cuts blocking from 300 ms to nanoseconds.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) long critical section from rebuilding while holding the lock; (b) reader contention on a single monitor; (c) GC pauses from the rebuild (red herring until checked in GC logs); (d) DB latency.
  4. How I'd verify each: JFR "Java Monitor Blocked" events; async-profiler -e lock; GC logs for pauses; compare p99 after the change in a k6 or wrk load test.
  5. Root cause: Reads and the long rebuild share one monitor.
  6. Fix: Immutable snapshot with atomic swap:
final class RateService {
    private volatile Map<String, Rate> table = Map.of();
    void refresh() {
        Map<String, Rate> fresh = loadAll();          // build off the hot path
        table = Map.copyOf(fresh);                    // immutable, then publish
    }
    Rate get(String k) { return table.get(k); }       // lock-free read
}

The volatile write publishes a fully built immutable map; the readers' volatile read gives the edge. For per-request consistency, read table once into a local at the request start. 7. Prevention: JFR lock-blocking alert; a rule that heavy work does not run inside locks. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The swap doubles memory briefly (two tables, 50k entries is small, but for GBs consider incremental updates). I would not use ConcurrentHashMap in-place updates if readers need a consistent whole-table view; ReadWriteLock doesn't remove the writer's 300 ms stall.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if a refresh needs to be incremental (updates every 100 ms)? → Persistent/structural-sharing maps, or ConcurrentHashMap with per-key versions and accept per-key consistency.
  • What if the DB is down? → Keep serving the old snapshot; do not publish a partial result.
  • Where could the 2-version memory spike hurt? → Container limit with a large table; check peak heap in GC logs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team solved this with ReadWriteLock; readers were fine until a refresh took 4 seconds during a DB incident and write-lock fairness queued all reads behind it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests more threads or caching elsewhere.
  • Hire: swap-reference pattern with volatile and immutable map.
  • Strong hire: explains the happens-before edge, local-read-once consistency, failure handling, and the memory spike trade-off.

questions.promptHtml: What is false sharing, how does it affect JVM programs, and how do @Contended and padding address it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know the memory model from people who also understand cache-coherence performance. Common in low-latency and metrics code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CPUs move memory in cache lines, typically 64 bytes. If two threads write different variables that happen to share a line, each write invalidates the other core's copy, so throughput collapses even though there is no logical sharing. In Java you fix it by padding or by @Contended, which makes the JVM pad the field or class to separate cache lines. It costs memory, and user code needs -XX:-RestrictContended.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The MESI-style coherence protocol gives a core exclusive ownership of a line to write it. Two cores alternately writing adjacent longs bounce the line back and forth: each write turns into a cross-core transfer (order of 100 ns on some multi-socket systems, verify with your hardware) instead of an L1 hit.

JEP 142 introduced the idea of marking contended fields so the VM keeps them off shared lines. In the JDK, @jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended (Java 9+; sun.misc.Contended in Java 8) is honoured for JDK classes; application classes need -XX:-RestrictContended. The padding default is controlled by -XX:ContendedPaddingWidth (default 128 bytes, verify for your version). The JDK itself uses it in LongAdder's Striped64.Cell, and ConcurrentHashMap's counter cells; Thread also has contended fields.

Manual padding alternatives: pad with unused longs (fragile because the JVM can reorder fields), or use arrays with stride (e.g. index i * 16 for 64-bit slots). Object layout is not specified, so verify with JOL.

Cache line (64B): | counterA (T1 writes) | counterB (T2 writes) | ...
T1 write -> invalidates T2's line -> T2 write -> invalidates T1's line ...
Fixed:     | counterA | pad ... |  | counterB | pad ... |  (separate lines)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Requires -XX:-RestrictContended outside the JDK
import jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended; // needs --add-exports java.base/jdk.internal.vm.annotation=ALL-UNNAMED
class Counters {
    @Contended volatile long a;
    @Contended volatile long b;
}
// Portable alternative: use LongAdder (stripes + @Contended cells internally)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Padding with fields and trusting layout without checking JOL.
  • Applying @Contended everywhere, wasting memory (128 bytes per annotated field).
  • Diagnosing it as "lock contention" because no locks appear in profiles.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you detect false sharing? → perf c2c on Linux, or throughput that does not scale with threads while CPU is high and no locks.
  2. What is true sharing? → Threads genuinely need the same variable; padding doesn't help.
  3. Why does LongAdder help? → Spreads updates over padded cells so threads rarely share a line.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "padding fields". Senior: cache-line mechanics, @Contended requirements and flags, JOL verification, perf c2c, and prefers LongAdder/sharding to hand-padding.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Per-thread metrics counters allocated in one long[] capped throughput at 4 cores of benefit on a 32-core box until each counter was moved to its own line.

questions.contextHtml:
A request-metrics component keeps per-worker counters in one array so the exporter can sum them cheaply:

final class Metrics {
    private final long[] perThread = new long[64];   // index = workerId, each worker writes only its slot
    void inc(int workerId) { perThread[workerId]++; }  // plain, single-writer per slot
    long total() { long s = 0; for (long v : perThread) s += v; return s; }
}

At 4 workers it handles 40M increments/s total. Moving to a 32-core host with 32 workers, throughput is 55M/s total, not the ~320M/s expected; CPU shows 100% across cores, no lock contention in JFR, GC is idle. The team wants to 10x traffic next quarter.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it not scale, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make them AtomicLong" (worse: still adjacent), or "threads fight over a lock" when there is none.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are slots strictly single-writer? How fresh must total() be? Is the slot count fixed? What is the cache-line size of the target CPU?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce the number of hot writers via batching in a thread-local accumulator and flush every N events, which buys time.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) false sharing: 8 longs share a 64-byte line, so 8 workers contend per line; (b) NUMA effects across sockets; (c) the total() read frequency; (d) JIT issue (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify each: perf c2c record/report on Linux for cache-line contention; a JMH benchmark comparing stride 1 vs stride 16; check CPU topology with lscpu; JOL if using objects.
  5. Root cause: Adjacent slots live on the same 64-byte line. Every increment needs exclusive ownership of the line, so cores bounce it. There is no logical sharing, but physical sharing causes the stall.
  6. Fix: Short-term, a stride so each worker's slot is on its own line, e.g. perThread[workerId * 16] (16 longs = 128 bytes, covering adjacent-line prefetchers). Long-term, use LongAdder per metric (its cells use @Contended) or per-thread counters flushed in batches.
private final long[] perThread = new long[64 * 16];
void inc(int id) { perThread[id * 16]++; }

For visibility of total(), reads see stale values unless there is an edge; for metrics, approximate reads are acceptable, but document it, or use VarHandle.getOpaque. 7. Prevention: A scaling benchmark (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 threads) in CI; rule that per-thread data structures be padded or sharded. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Padding costs memory (128 bytes per counter); I would not apply it to every counter, only hot ones. I would not use synchronized.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would AtomicLongArray fix it? → No; same layout, atomics just add cost.
  • Why 128 and not 64? → Adjacent-line prefetching on some Intel parts; JDK default padding is 128 bytes (verify for your version).
  • Does false sharing happen on ARM too? → Yes; line sizes vary (64B common; some are 128B).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A queue's head and tail indices sat in one object; adding @Contended to each doubled throughput at 8 producers. The same trick on 100 unrelated fields later bloated every object by 12 KB.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames locks or GC without evidence.
  • Hire: identifies false sharing and pads or uses LongAdder.
  • Strong hire: uses perf c2c, explains line size and prefetcher reasoning, weighs memory cost and visibility semantics of the result.

questions.promptHtml: What are the VarHandle access modes (plain, opaque, acquire/release, volatile), and when would you use release/acquire instead of volatile?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth beyond volatile and tells whether you can read JDK concurrency source (queues, AtomicX.lazySet). Typically asked of staff-level candidates.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Access modes form a hierarchy of increasing guarantees: plain (no ordering, any reordering or elimination), opaque (per-variable coherence and eventual visibility, but no cross-variable ordering), release/acquire (a release write is ordered after earlier accesses and an acquire read before later ones, so message passing works), and volatile (all of that plus a single total order, i.e. sequential consistency). Use release/acquire for single-writer publication patterns where you do not need a total order across threads; it is cheaper than volatile on weak hardware and avoids the StoreLoad barrier on x86.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From Doug Lea's guide to the JDK 9 memory model modes:

Mode Methods Guarantees
Plain get/set only type safety and in-thread precedence
Opaque getOpaque/setOpaque coherence per variable, progress (a spin read terminates), bitwise atomic 64-bit
Release/Acquire setRelease/getAcquire causality: producer's earlier writes visible after consumer's acquire sees the release
Volatile setVolatile/getVolatile total order of volatile accesses, prevents Dekker-style both-read-zero

Message-passing pattern (works with release/acquire):

Producer: data = 42 (plain); flag.setRelease(1)
Consumer: if (flag.getAcquire() == 1) read data -> 42

What release/acquire does not give: store-buffering protection. In Dekker-style flags where both threads write their flag then read the other's, release/acquire allows both to read 0; volatile forbids it. So use volatile for mutual-exclusion algorithms and consensus.

AtomicX.lazySet is setRelease. JDK queues (for example ConcurrentLinkedQueue) use VarHandles to avoid full barriers. Compare-and-set variants: compareAndSet, weakCompareAndSet*, compareAndExchange*, getAndAdd.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import java.lang.invoke.*;

class SpscSlot {
    private static final VarHandle READY;
    static {
        try { READY = MethodHandles.lookup().findVarHandle(SpscSlot.class, "ready", int.class); }
        catch (ReflectiveOperationException e) { throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(e); }
    }
    private int ready;      // accessed only via READY
    private long payload;   // plain, ordered by release/acquire
    void publish(long v) { payload = v; READY.setRelease(this, 1); }
    Long poll() { return ((int) READY.getAcquire(this) == 1) ? payload : null; }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using plain get of a field that other threads write via setRelease.
  • Choosing release/acquire for Dekker-style algorithms.
  • Reaching for VarHandle when volatile or AtomicX is enough; the complexity is a maintenance cost.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does opaque guarantee that plain does not? → Progress and coherence; an opaque spin loop cannot be hoisted forever.
  2. Why is release/acquire cheaper on x86? → Ordinary loads and stores already provide it; no StoreLoad barrier needed.
  3. Where in the JDK is it used? → AtomicX.lazySet, many java.util.concurrent classes via VarHandle (replaces Unsafe).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: never heard of VarHandle. Senior: states the hierarchy, message-passing and its limits, and says when not to use it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom single-producer ring buffer switched the sequence update to setRelease, removing a full fence per message; throughput improved measurably, but only after a jcstress check proved the consumer never saw stale payloads.

questions.promptHtml: What does the JMM actually promise for a correctly synchronized program, and what does it promise for a program with data races?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the formal contract behind everything. Staff-level engineers should know that "racy" is not "undefined behaviour" in Java.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If a program has no data races in its sequentially consistent executions, then all its executions appear sequentially consistent (SC-DRF). That is the simple model you should program to. For racy programs, Java still gives safety: no out-of-thin-air values, type safety, no memory corruption, and a read sees either the default value or some write that is not ordered after it by happens-before. But the exact value is unpredictable, and non-volatile long/double can tear.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
JLS 17.4.3 defines correctly synchronized programs and promises SC. JLS 17.4.5 says a read may observe any write that is not ordered after it and is not overwritten in happens-before. The causality rules (17.4.8) forbid values from appearing from nowhere, as in the classic example where each thread's write is justified only by the other's read; the standard racy example allows r1 == 1 && r2 == 2 via reordering but not invented constants. Shipilev describes the commit-based causality rules as intricate and a known pain point.

Contrast with C/C++: a data race is undefined behaviour there; in Java the worst case is surprising but bounded values. Even so, relying on benign races is fragile (JIT may hoist, merge or eliminate accesses; String.hashCode is a documented deliberate benign race using a final-safe pattern).

Practical reading: design so every shared mutable access is covered by an edge; if you intentionally use races, document the invariants you rely on (idempotent computation, immutable result).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// String.hashCode style benign race: idempotent, int atomic, result immutable
class Lazy {
    private int hash;                 // 0 means not computed
    int hash() {
        int h = hash;                 // read once
        if (h == 0) { h = compute(); hash = h; }
        return h;
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating "race" with "undefined behaviour" like C++.
  • Using benign races with non-idempotent or non-atomic types (e.g. racy long, mutable object).
  • Reading a racy field twice and expecting the same value.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is an out-of-thin-air value? → A value no thread ever wrote, justified only circularly; forbidden by causality rules.
  2. Why does String.hashCode work with a race? → Idempotent result, int write is atomic, value same regardless of which thread computes it.
  3. Is a racy singleton read safe? → Not unless the published object is safely initialized, e.g. all final fields.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "races make things undefined". Senior: SC-DRF, bounded racy behaviour, causality, and conditions for deliberate benign races.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A lazily computed cached BigDecimal field with racy publication returned an object seen in a partially initialized state on ARM until the class made its fields final.

questions.contextHtml:
A company migrated a checkout service from x86 (c5.2xlarge, 8 vCPU) to ARM (Graviton, 8 vCPU) nodes for ~20% cost savings, same JDK 17 build, same traffic (2,500 RPS). Within a day, 1 in ~3M requests failed with NullPointerException in ShippingRules.apply or applied rate 0.0. It had never occurred on x86 in 18 months. Heap is healthy, GC pause p99 is 12 ms, no deploys changed code. The class:

class ShippingRules {
    double baseRate; Map<String,Double> zones;   // plain fields
    ShippingRules(Loader l) { baseRate = l.base(); zones = l.zones(); }
}
class RuleHolder { static ShippingRules current; // plain static
    static void refresh() { current = new ShippingRules(loader); } }
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident review: cause, why now, fix, and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ARM JVM bug" or "retry on NPE"; no use of the memory model; blames the loader.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the failure correlate only with the ARM nodes? Within seconds after a refresh? Which JDK flags differ? Is current read by many request threads?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin the service back to x86 nodes via scheduling, or make current volatile as a one-line hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) unsafe publication of ShippingRules through a plain static; (b) a loader returning null occasionally (red herring: logs show the loader returns non-null); (c) JIT bug (unlikely); (d) heap corruption (no evidence).
  4. How I'd verify each: Correlate error timestamps with refresh() times from logs; reproduce with a jcstress test on an ARM machine; check that failures vanish with volatile in a canary.
  5. Root cause: Writing current is a plain store; the constructor's field writes and the store can be reordered or become visible out of order on the weakly ordered ARM memory model. Readers see non-null current with default baseRate = 0.0 or null zones. x86's stronger ordering (stores stay ordered with other stores) hid this; Shipilev's tests found unsafe publication failing on ARM while nearly never on x86.
  6. Fix: Make fields final and publish through a volatile:
final class ShippingRules {
    final double baseRate; final Map<String,Double> zones;
    ShippingRules(Loader l) { baseRate = l.base(); zones = Map.copyOf(l.zones()); }
}
class RuleHolder { private static volatile ShippingRules current; ... }
  1. Prevention: Review rule: every cross-thread reference swap has a named edge; run concurrency tests (jcstress) on both architectures; CI architecture matrix before migrations.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just retry on NPE (masks bad 0.0 rate, which is wrong money); I would not say "ARM is flaky" in the review; the bug was always latent.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would making only the fields final be enough? → For the contents yes, but readers can still see null current momentarily; that is acceptable if handled.
  • Why did stress on x86 never show it? → TSO keeps stores ordered; compiler reordering was also unlikely for that code shape.
  • How would you prove the fix? → jcstress on ARM, plus canary error rates over millions of requests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration to a new CPU generation surfaced three latent publication bugs in a week; the team added an "architecture parity" soak test to the migration checklist.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames platform or adds retries.
  • Hire: identifies unsafe publication and fixes with volatile/final.
  • Strong hire: explains memory-model difference between architectures, proposes jcstress and migration checklist, argues against masking the symptom.

questions.contextHtml:
A feature-flag cache keeps its enabled flags in a volatile array and a background poller flips entries. Request threads occasionally keep serving a disabled feature for minutes after the poller updated it (poll log says "flag payments_v2 -> off at 10:04:11", requests at 10:09 still use it, on a few pods only).

class Flags {
    private volatile boolean[] enabled = new boolean[256];
    boolean isOn(int id) { return enabled[id]; }
    void set(int id, boolean v) { enabled[id] = v; }   // called from poller
}

Pods: 12, 4 vCPU, JDK 17.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug and what are the correct designs?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Volatile is on the field, so it must be a cache TTL or poller failure."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the stale pod keep stale values forever or just a while? Is anything else reading the array? Is the array ever replaced?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart affected pods; as hotfix swap the array wholesale (new array each poll) via the volatile field.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) volatile applies to the reference, not elements, so element writes are plain; (b) poller failure on those pods (logs say it ran); (c) CDN or config source skew (red herring, same poll source); (d) JIT hoisting of enabled[id] read in a hot loop.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check the poller log on a stale pod; JFR to see the hot method compiled; test with a loop reading isOn while another thread sets; try replacing with AtomicIntegerArray in a canary.
  5. Root cause: volatile boolean[] makes reads and writes of the array reference volatile, not the elements. enabled[id] = v is a plain store with no happens-before to reads; a JIT-compiled hot reader can reuse a loaded value.
  6. Fix: Options: (1) immutable snapshot, new array per poll then enabled = fresh (volatile write publishes it); (2) AtomicIntegerArray / AtomicReferenceArray with volatile element semantics; (3) VarHandle for array elements via MethodHandles.arrayElementVarHandle and setVolatile/getVolatile; (4) ConcurrentHashMap<String,Boolean>.
private volatile boolean[] enabled = new boolean[256];
void replace(boolean[] fresh) { enabled = fresh.clone(); }     // publish a snapshot
boolean isOn(int id) { return enabled[id]; }                    // one volatile read of ref
  1. Prevention: Review rule: "volatile on arrays/collections never protects contents"; a SpotBugs check (VO_VOLATILE_REFERENCE_TO_ARRAY).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Snapshot allocates 256 bytes per poll, negligible. I would not add synchronized to the read path.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not just volatile on each element? → Java has no per-element volatile syntax; use atomic arrays or VarHandle.
  • Does the snapshot approach guarantee all flags change together? → Yes, readers see one consistent array.
  • Is AtomicIntegerArray slower? → Volatile access per element; negligible for flags, matters at high write rates.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "emergency kill switch" implemented as volatile Map with in-place put worked in tests and failed in the one incident it was meant for.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames network/poller.
  • Hire: explains volatile applies to the reference only, fixes with snapshot or atomic array.
  • Strong hire: knows SpotBugs/VarHandle options and consistency benefits of snapshots.

questions.promptHtml: How do you test or prove that concurrent code is correct under the JMM? Why do ordinary unit and stress tests fail to catch memory-model bugs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors must know the limits of testing and the right tools; "I ran it with 100 threads" is a red flag.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Memory-model bugs depend on the JIT, CPU architecture and timing, so ordinary tests pass for years. I reason by happens-before: for each shared variable I name the edge between every write and read. To test, I use jcstress, the OpenJDK harness that runs small actor tests millions of times and tabulates the outcomes, on the real target architectures. I also use static analysis and review checklists, and I prefer designs (immutability, confinement, locks) that make reasoning easy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why plain tests fail:

  • x86 TSO hides most reordering; ARM exposes it (Shipilev measured zero failures on x86 for many unsafe patterns vs hundreds per 100M tries on ARMv7).
  • Failure windows are nanoseconds wide and only appear after C2 compiles and inlines.
  • Test harness synchronization (printing, queues) adds accidental edges.

jcstress style: define @Actor methods, an @Arbiter, and an expected outcome table (ACCEPTABLE, FORBIDDEN, ACCEPTABLE_INTERESTING). It forces JIT variations and varies thread placement. It tests small, isolated protocols, not whole services.

Reasoning method: for every shared field write the "who writes, who reads, which edge" table. Confined data (thread-local, stack) needs none. Immutable data needs only safe publication of the reference.

Other tools: SpotBugs/ErrorProne rules, -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions stress flags used in research (verify before using any), and JMH for performance not correctness.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// jcstress sketch (org.openjdk.jcstress): check publication via plain field
@JCStressTest
@Outcome(id = "0, 0", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "not yet published")
@Outcome(id = "1, 42", expect = ACCEPTABLE, desc = "published and visible")
@Outcome(id = "1, 0", expect = FORBIDDEN, desc = "ready but stale data")
@State
public class PublishTest {
    int data; volatile int ready;
    @Actor public void writer() { data = 42; ready = 1; }
    @Actor public void reader(II_Result r) { r.r1 = ready; r.r2 = (r.r1 == 1) ? data : 0; }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "It passed 10,000 iterations" as proof.
  • Testing only on one architecture and JDK build.
  • Adding println to the test, which synchronizes and masks the bug.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does jcstress add over JUnit? → Controlled interleavings at scale and outcome classification, including JIT and architecture effects.
  2. Can you prove DCL is safe by testing? → No; you prove it with edges, and tests only add evidence.
  3. How do you keep this maintainable on a team? → Prefer immutable snapshots and well-known idioms; keep exotic code isolated and covered with jcstress.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "write a multithreaded test". Senior: reason by edges first, test with jcstress on target hardware, and design to avoid the need.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bug that survived 3 years of CI appeared after a hardware refresh; a 20-line jcstress test reproduced it in under a minute on the new platform.

questions.contextHtml:
A code review lands on your desk. Author's note: "p99 on /quote is 40 ms and profiling shows synchronized on QuoteCache.get; I removed the locks since reads are safe and writes are rare, 5 writes/min vs 9,000 reads/s." Diff:

class QuoteCache {
    private final HashMap<String, Quote> map = new HashMap<>();
    private Quote latest;                                   // was guarded by this
    public Quote get(String k) { return map.get(k); }       // lock removed
    public void put(String k, Quote q) { synchronized (this) { map.put(k, q); latest = q; } }
    public Quote latest() { return latest; }                // lock removed
}

The author also says "p99 improved 12 ms in the benchmark".
questions.promptHtml: Do you approve it? What do you say, and what do you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, writes are rare" or "reject, always use locks"; no concrete failure mode or alternative.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How was the benchmark run (JMH or ad hoc), on which architecture, with concurrent writers? What is the actual contention (35% blocked time or just uncontended lock overhead)? Do readers need a consistent pair of map and latest?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the merge; the change is unsafe. If the lock really is the p99 problem, deliver a safe quick fix instead.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (about the p99): (a) readers block behind a writer holding the lock; but writes are 5/min so unlikely to explain p99; (b) the lock itself is cheap uncontended; (c) real p99 comes from elsewhere (GC, downstream); (d) benchmark noise.
  4. How I'd verify each: JFR lock events (jdk.JavaMonitorEnter) to see whether threads were blocked; async-profiler wall-clock mode; rerun with JMH under concurrent read/write.
  5. Root cause of the risk: HashMap is not safe for a reader concurrent with a writer: without an edge, readers can see stale or inconsistent state; during a resize, a reader can miss entries (and older JDKs had resize-related infinite loops in concurrent mutation; verify for your version, the JDK 8+ implementation avoids the classic loop but is still unsupported). latest is a plain field with no edge. Both are data races.
  6. Fix: A ConcurrentHashMap for the map and volatile for latest, or better an immutable snapshot swapped on writes (5 writes/min makes copying cheap):
class QuoteCache {
    private volatile Map<String, Quote> snap = Map.of();
    private volatile Quote latest;
    Quote get(String k) { return snap.get(k); }
    synchronized void put(String k, Quote q) {
        var m = new HashMap<>(snap); m.put(k, q);
        snap = Map.copyOf(m); latest = q;
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Require a JMH or jcstress artifact for any PR that removes synchronization; checklist item "which edge makes this read safe".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not accept "writes are rare" as a safety argument; rarity reduces frequency but not possibility, and on a production incident it will be the worst moment. ConcurrentHashMap is simpler if consistency across the map is not needed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if writes were 5,000/s? → Snapshot copy becomes costly; use ConcurrentHashMap or a persistent map.
  • Does latest and snap read as a pair stay consistent? → Not unless they are one immutable holder object.
  • What if the benchmark showed no benefit from removing locks? → Even more reason to reject; also confirms the lock was not the p99 source.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "rarely written" HashMap cache held up for two years, then a resize during a traffic spike caused intermittent missed lookups, which looked like downstream failures for a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves, or rejects without a mechanism.
  • Hire: names data race and provides a safe alternative.
  • Strong hire: challenges the performance claim with data, proposes snapshot design with composite consistency, and sets a review standard for lock removal.
